title: Shearing's contact with Cuban rhythm
summary: Shearing hears his band, hires a conga player, and develops his quintet.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Now, for the first time, he come in contact with the Cuban rhythm, right there in my band. He used to scratch his eye with his finger and listen. Oh, (unintelligible) what is that? And that's where he begin to get (inaudible). So then he had a conga player.

Almondo Perrassa. So he wanted Almondo to get Cuban music for him. So right away, when you tell a Cuban writer to get some music for George Shearing, right away, they (unintelligible) some other way. So they brought some tunes to him. So when he plays it, (unintelligible) every day. I want to be authentic Cuban tunes, I don't want (unintelligible). That ain't Cuban, that's jazz.
And I told Almondo, I said, right, throw away your people (unintelligible). And then after that, I lose track of him and I never saw him no more. I haven't seen him in years.
I remember the quintet style. He was playing with a vibes player, vibraphone, piano, --
After that he went to the -- like, a quintet like this guy on the coast.
Cheta. Well, Cheta started with him.
And then Cheta went by his own.
Did you hear the quintet style with the vibraphone and piano?
Well, I heard him in some records.
What did you think of that?

That was beautiful, and they started messing around with the bass. A guy by the name -- what's his name, that big, big (unintelligible). It was a big heavy guy from -- black guy, played bass. He tried to start playing the (unintelligible).
Yeah, they were trying to make changes. How good they did, how bad they did, I don't know, because I didn't follow it.
